prompt: what actually makes the tide come in and go out

prompt: why are there two high tides a day and not one
reply: Because the ocean bulges on both sides of Earth. The Moon's pull is strongest on the near ocean, weaker on Earth's centre, weakest on the far ocean — so the near water is pulled toward the Moon and the far water is effectively left behind. Two bulges, and you spin through both. 🌊 [QUIZ]Which ocean feels the Moon's pull most strongly?[/QUIZ][CHIPS]The near side|The far side|Both the same[/CHIPS]

prompt: if a planet had zero tilt would it have seasons
reply: Almost none. Seasons come from tilt: the half leaning sunward gets steeper, more concentrated sunlight and longer days. With zero tilt every latitude would get the same sunlight angle all year — twelve-hour days everywhere, poles stuck in permanent chilly twilight. You would still get a whisper of change if the orbit were oval, but nothing like winter. 🪐 [CHIPS]Any planet like that?|Does Mercury have seasons?|Does orbit shape matter?[/CHIPS]

prompt: what exactly happens at an equinox
reply: Twice a year — around 20 March and 22 September — Earth's tilt leans neither toward nor away from the Sun. The day-night line then runs straight through both poles, so everywhere gets close to twelve hours of daylight. The Sun rises almost due east and sets almost due west. Day still beats night by a few minutes, because our atmosphere bends sunlight over the horizon. ☀️ [FACT]Equinox comes from Latin words meaning equal night.[/FACT][CHIPS]Why not exactly twelve?|What is a solstice?|Find east at sunrise[/CHIPS]

prompt: what actually causes an aurora
reply: A chain that starts on the Sun. It flings out a stream of charged particles; Earth's magnetic field deflects most of them, but funnels some down along the field lines into the polar regions. About 100 km up they slam into oxygen and nitrogen atoms, pushing their electrons to higher energy levels. When those electrons drop back, the atom releases the light you see — oxygen green, nitrogen violet-blue. 💫 [CHIPS]Why only at poles?|What makes red aurora?|Aurora on other planets?[/CHIPS]

prompt: is there an aurora at the south pole too
reply: Yes — the aurora australis, and it is often close to a mirror image of the northern one. The same field lines thread both hemispheres, so particles arriving at one end usually arrive at the other, producing near-matching shapes at the same moment. Fewer people see it because there is mostly ocean and Antarctica down there; Tasmania and southern New Zealand get the best public view. 🧭 [CHIPS]Are they truly identical?|Best month to see?|Aurora from space station?[/CHIPS]

prompt: why do telescopes use mirrors instead of lenses
reply: Two reasons, both about size. 🔭 A big lens can only be held at its rim, so it sags under its own weight, while a mirror can be propped up across its whole back. Lenses also bend different colours by different amounts, leaving colour fringes; a mirror reflects every colour identically. 🪞 [CHIPS]Biggest telescope mirror?|What is a refractor?|Do mirrors need coating?[/CHIPS]

prompt: why put a telescope in space instead of on a mountain
reply: Because even the best mountain still sits under an atmosphere. Thin air still smudges the image, and it completely blocks some wavelengths — most infrared and ultraviolet never reach the ground. An infrared telescope also has to be brutally cold, or its own warmth drowns the signal, which is why James Webb hides behind a tennis-court-sized sunshield far from Earth. The price: nobody can pop up and repair it. 🔭 [CHIPS]Where exactly is Webb?|What did Hubble see?|Why infrared matters?[/CHIPS]
